To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the nitrate concentration in the River Thames at Hampton (London) is the longest continuous record in the world; 2) the nitrate concentrations at Hampton have been increasing steadily since the start of the 20th century; and, 3) the nitrate pollution in the River Thames is a consequence of agricultural intensification, which has resulted in an accumulation of reactive N species in the catchment. [2]

(1) the nitrate pollution problem has arisen due to the accumulation of a reactive N stock in the catchment; (2) the size of the stock is unknown; (3) the stock is likely to be in the order of 100 kt N yr− 1; (4) the stock will take decades to be reduced by natural processes alone; and (5) the stock will only be reduced by human intervention.
(i) 20th century increases in land use intensity have led to an accumulation in the catchment of 100 (40) kt N, which is equivalent to a 2‐fold increase in the amount of reactive N in the catchment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question “What are the prospects for restoring high-quality groundwater in the face of continuing agricultural intensification?”

the long-term sustainability of groundwater quality, and in this context the term ‘sustainable’ is defined as the ability to maintain the current quality into the future, and not to return to the preintensifying conditions of the early 20th century.
the question: “How can we sustainably manage groundwater quality in the face of the increasing demand for food?”
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the River Thames is not a “natural” system.
the nitrate pollution of groundwater in the Thames catchment is now so extensive that it cannot be reversed by current policy and management approaches. [2]
, for the Thames catchment, the prospects for sustaining groundwater quality are poor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are not in control of nitrate in our groundwater.
we need to accept that we have already lost the battle against nitrate pollution, and we need to move to strategies for living with it. [2]
we are now at the point where we can no longer sustain high-quality groundwater in intensively farmland. [2]
The main takeaway from our work is that
the long-term storage of reactive N species in the aquifer means that the prospects for restoring water-quality to the preintensified levels are poor.
the nitrate problem in the Thames catchment is now so large that we need a new approach to the problem that is based on a long‐term strategy.
it is possible to develop a long-term record of nitrate pollution in a large, intensively farmed catchment, and to use that to explore the prospects for restoration of water quality.
